fixes.explanation: Benaiah son of Jehoiada shows up later in David's story, as the man over the Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18). Good name to know, but he isn't the one at this pool. The text says Joab son of Zeruiah marches out with David's servants. Different name, different moment.

No kings are named in this scene. Abner speaks to Joab, and what he asks for is that the young men get up and compete before them. The talking at the pool is between those two. A sit-down would have been a very different afternoon.

Going home in peace would have been a short story, friend, and the text keeps going. Abner's words to Joab are, “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” That's his suggestion, and it has nothing to do with going home.
Twelve it is. The young men are counted off, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. Twelve and twelve. I'd have counted twice, just to feel useful.
Forty, friend? I'd need a second mustache just to count that high. The text says they were counted off, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. That's twelve a side.

Not quite. Each man grabs his opponent and thrusts his sword into his opponent's side, and then “…they all fell together.” When everyone falls together, there's no side left standing to call the winner. Then the text says, “The battle that day was intense…”

Asahel chases Abner, and the text says he never turns to the right or to the left while he does it. He is one of the three sons of Zeruiah, and the text calls him fleet of foot like a wild gazelle. Out of everyone on that field, he picks Abner and sticks with him.

Ish-bosheth son of Saul is named in this passage, but the chase isn't aimed at him. The text sends Abner and the servants of Ish-bosheth out to Gibeon, and then Asahel chases Abner. So the name that goes in the blank is Abner.
The Benjamites rally to Abner, form a single unit, and take their stand atop a hill. Joab and Abishai are pursuing Abner, and his side comes together as one group. Then Abner calls out to Joab.

Joab says the opposite. His words are, “if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” So Abner speaking up is what changes things. By sunset, the text says, they had gone as far as the hill of Ammah.
Right. Joab blows the ram's horn, and all the troops stop. The text says they “…no longer pursued Israel or continued to fight.” The horn sounds and the fighting stops.

They bury Asahel in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. The text calls it his father's tomb and puts it in Bethlehem. After the burial, Joab and his men march all night. The text tells us this and nothing more about it.

Gibeon is where the pool is, and where the fighting happened. Asahel is buried somewhere else. The text says David's men took him and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. So the burial is in Bethlehem, not at Gibeon.

Only one side is growing weaker. The text says David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. Two sides, two different directions. David's side is the one getting stronger.
